written.q: Explain latency vs throughput and describe caching and load balancing as performance tools.
written.a: Latency is how long one operation takes for one user; throughput is how much work the system does per unit time. Caching stores the result of expensive reads so later requests are answered in about 1 ms; cache read-often, change-rarely data and manage invalidation. A load balancer spreads requests over servers, health-checks them and hides failures, but requires any server to answer any request.

written.q: Explain why stateless servers enable horizontal scaling and how sessions are handled.
written.a: If servers keep per-user state in memory, a request routed to another instance finds no session. Making requests carry everything needed (a token on every request) means any instance can answer any request, so machines can be added behind a load balancer. Sessions are handled with a shared session store such as Redis or with stateless tokens (JWT) verified locally.

written.q: Describe reliability: availability nines, single points of failure and the timeout, retry and circuit-breaker tools.
written.a: Availability is uptime over total time: 99.9 % allows 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99 % 53 minutes. Remove single points of failure with redundancy (several app servers, DB primary and replica). Partial failure is handled with timeouts (deadline on every call), retries (idempotent operations only, limited with backoff) and a circuit breaker (after repeated failures open and fail fast to a fallback, probing in a half-open state).

written.q: List security measures an architect should apply, including the first rule and how to stop SQL injection.
written.a: Authentication and server-side authorisation on every request; never trust the client (validate everything on the server); HTTPS/TLS in transit; encryption at rest including backups; passwords hashed with bcrypt/argon2; parameterised queries against SQL injection; secrets in environment variables, never in Git, with a committed .env.example.

written.q: Choose a data store for orders and payments, restaurant menus, carts and GPS pings, with reasons.
written.a: Orders and payments: SQL (joins, integrity, transactions). Menus: document store (nested, flexible shape, read whole). Carts and sessions: key-value such as Redis (tiny, by key, expiring, instant). GPS pings: wide-column such as Cassandra (huge append-only write volume). Choose per data shape, not one DB for the whole system.
